[PAPER_0014, relevance_score=0.289] Action Plan Discarding

In the current study, we investigated what happens to action plans when they are discarded before execution. Such action plan discarding is a vital component of behavioral flexibility. It occurs when an initial action plan cannot, need not, or must not, be carried out anymore.

[PAPER_0016, relevance_score=0.301] To this end, we conducted two experiments in which we modified the tried-and-tested ABBA paradigm (Mocke et al., 2022). Both experiments shared the same basic experimental procedure (Figure 1). Participants were shown a first Stimulus A that indicated which Action A to plan. Action A was either a short or a long keypress with the left or the right hand. Importantly, we then included a continue/discard signal that indicated whether to carry on with planning Action A (75% of the trials) or to discard that action (25%).

[PAPER_0033, relevance_score=0.307] Transparency and Openness

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the studies. All raw data from an online pilot study and both experiments described here, analyses scripts, experimental material, and supplementary analyses are openly available at the open science framework (Mocke, Beste, et al., 2023, https://osf.io/3dky6/). Data were analyzed using R, Version 4.0.0 (R Core Team, 2021).

[PAPER_0089, relevance_score=0.284] In Experiment 2 though, these signs of feature binding (i.e., no overlap being worse than full overlap and partial overlap being worse than no overlap) were at least descriptively apparent after discarding. Still, the post hoc tests of action-specific suppression provided evidence that feature unbinding did take place after the discard signal, as shown by a reduced difference between partial and no overlap trials (see Figure 2, prediction 2.1), at least with longer discard time.

[PAPER_0096, relevance_score=0.291] General Discussion

What happens when a formed action plan is discarded? Derived from the assumption that action plans rest on temporarily binding codes of action features to a unique combination, we tested the idea that discarding a planned action would prompt unbinding of these features. To this end, we conducted two experiments, in which in a minority of trials a signal suggested to participants to discard an already formed action plan. We reasoned that any remaining feature binding would be indicated by costs of initiating another action that shares some instead of all features or neither feature with the concurrently planned action.

[PAPER_0104, relevance_score=0.294] Our data, however, show the exact opposite pattern. To conclude, both procedural as well as empirical considerations support the assumption that action plan A had been formed prior to the signal onset in discard trials.

[PAPER_0120, relevance_score=0.313] Importantly, previous studies differ to ours in the sense that we investigated the altering of not yet experienced but merely prepared action files.

Turning to the latter, our findings seem to be somewhat at odds with observations on the persistence of SR bindings for delayed intentions. In such paradigms, participants are instructed to maintain SR links ("If S, then do R") for later use.

[PAPER_0125, relevance_score=0.290] Conclusion

Taken together, the two presented experiments both yielded data that are in line with unbinding of action features after discarding an action plan. This shows that (un)binding as a process is apparently not only involved in action plan construction, but also in action plan deconstruction. This significantly broadens the relevance of binding mechanism to various instances of behavioral control.

[PREREG_0007, relevance_score=0.335] The main hypothesis is that partial overlap costs (i.e., the difference between partial overlap and no/full overlap conditions) will be larger in continue than in discard trials. Possibly, the discard signal triggers the unbinding (disintegration) of still-activated features of action A. If no binding exists anymore, no retrieval of still-bound features can occur. Instead, there might be even overlap-benefits which might be stronger the more activated, but no more bound, overlapping features there are, hence with full as compared to partial overlap.

[PREREG_0008, relevance_score=0.374] A pilot study (n = 20) indeed yielded reduced partial overlap costs as well as general speeding in discard as compared to continue trials. With respect to the discard time manipulation we derived the following hypothesis: Discard processes should have a higher chance to operate the more time they have to unfold, which should lead to relatively fewer traces of partial overlap costs the longer the interval between discard signal and stimulus B. Thus, partial overlap costs should be smaller with more discard time.

Therefore, we collected a total of n = 52 participants (Mdnage = 25, range = 19-62, 12 men, 40 women, 46 right-handed, four left-handed, two nonanswers. Mdnduration = 49.82 min for Session 1, Mdnduration = 57.5 min for Session 2).

[PAPER_0123, relevance_score=0.396] Constraints on Generality

With respect to generality, we note that we relied on a nonrepresentative sample of participants and used a specific setting to examine action plan discarding. Our sample of participants consisted of German-speaking, mostly young, female, Caucasian, and neurotypical participants from the same region with an interest in psychological research and willing to take part in a rather long and possibly tedious laboratory study.

[PAPER_0124, relevance_score=0.353] Furthermore, our experimental material consisted of very simple visual stimuli only, we used a laboratory environment, and the decision to discard an action plan was not made by the participants themselves but they were given an instruction. Whether our findings can be generalized to larger-scale action plans (e.g., discarding the plan to raise one's hand after someone else has asked the same question) might be a topic for future research. Varying such aspects might yield more insights into discarding processes under different circumstances and in more diverse populations.

[PREREG_0004, relevance_score=0.284] How a discarded action A impacts the initiation of a feature-overlapping action B conceivably depends on two factors, the time already spent on planning action A before discarding, and the time after discarding action A, but before the requested action B.
